overview.title: NaiveSequential: chaining layers into a mock Keras model
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.5 Looking back at our first example
overview.subsection: 2.5.1 Reimplementing our first example from scratch
overview.main_topic: The weights property of NaiveDense, the NaiveSequential class that chains layers and collects their weights, the mock MNIST model 784 -> 512 (relu) -> 10 (softmax), and the start of a batch generator
overview.central_idea: A sequential model is just a list of layers applied in order, plus a way to gather all their parameters. With NaiveDense and NaiveSequential, the Keras model from p.76 becomes a plain Python object whose four weight tensors (W and b of each layer) are explicitly listed, ready to be updated by a hand-written training step.
overview.importance: Collecting the weights into one list is what makes a generic training step possible: gradients will be computed with respect to model.weights and applied to model.weights (p.79-p.80). The mock model reproduces exactly the architecture of the first example.
learning_objectives: Explain the purpose of the weights property in NaiveDense and NaiveSequential.
Build the mock MNIST model and explain why it has exactly 4 weight tensors and what their shapes are.
Explain why a batch generator is needed to iterate over MNIST in mini-batches.
prerequisites: NaiveDense, keras.Variable and the Dense formula (p.77)

summary:
The page opens with the last three lines of `NaiveDense` (begun on p.77): a `weights` property returning `[self.W, self.b]`, which the callout calls *the convenience method for retrieving the layer's weights*.

**A simple Sequential class.** `NaiveSequential` chains layers. Its constructor stores a list of layers; its `__call__()` starts from `x = inputs` and replaces `x` by `layer(x)` for each layer in order, returning the final `x`. A `weights` property loops over the layers and concatenates their `weights` lists, so the model's parameters can be tracked easily.

**The mock Keras model.** With the two classes, the authors rebuild the first example's architecture:

- `NaiveDense(input_size=28 * 28, output_size=512, activation=ops.relu)`
- `NaiveDense(input_size=512, output_size=10, activation=ops.softmax)`

and check `assert len(model.weights) == 4`: two layers times (W, b). The shapes are (784, 512), (512,), (512, 10) and (10,), i.e. 407,050 scalars in total (count computed for these notes).

**A batch generator.** Next comes a way to iterate over MNIST in mini-batches, described as easy. The page shows only the start, `import math` and `class BatchGenerator:` with `def __init__(self, images, labels, batch_size=128):`; the body continues on p.79, where it stores the data, an index and `num_batches = math.ceil(len(images) / batch_size)`, and a `next()` method slices out the next batch.

Compared with Keras, the mock model must be told input sizes explicitly and keeps its weights in a hand-assembled list, but conceptually it is the same object as `keras.Sequential([...])` on p.76.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, let’s create a NaiveSequential class to chain these layers. It wraps
paragraphs.what_it_says: NaiveSequential wraps a list of layers, exposes a __call__() method that calls the underlying layers on the inputs in order, and has a weights property to keep track of the layers' parameters.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model is the composition f(x) = layer_n(...layer_2(layer_1(x))). Because each NaiveDense is itself callable, the model does not need to know anything about what a layer computes, only that it maps a tensor to a tensor. The weights property flattens the per-layer lists [W1, b1] and [W2, b2] into one list [W1, b1, W2, b2], which is the form the gradient computation and the update step need.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the minimal structure of every Keras model: a forward computation plus an enumerable set of trainable variables. Training code can be written once against model(x) and model.weights, independently of the architecture.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The list concatenation `weights += layer.weights` preserves order, so gradients returned for model.weights later line up one-to-one with the variables.

concepts.name: Sequential model
concepts.definition: A model that applies a list of layers in order; here NaiveSequential.
concepts.intuition: An assembly line: each station transforms the item and passes it on.
concepts.technical: __call__: x = inputs; for layer in layers: x = layer(x); return x.
concepts.significance: Reproduces keras.Sequential with a handful of lines.
concepts.misconception: The model does not hold its own parameters separately from the layers; its weights property just collects the layers' variables.

concepts.name: Model weights list
concepts.definition: The ordered list of all trainable variables of the model, obtained by concatenating each layer's weights.
concepts.intuition: An inventory of every knob the training process may turn.
concepts.significance: The argument passed to gradient computation and to the update step (p.79-p.80).
concepts.misconception: len(model.weights) counts tensors, not scalar parameters; there are 407,050 scalars in these 4 tensors.

concepts.name: Mini-batch iteration
concepts.definition: Splitting the training data into consecutive chunks of batch_size samples, each used for one training step.
concepts.intuition: Reading a book a few pages at a time instead of all at once.
concepts.technical: With batch_size=128 and 60,000 images there are math.ceil(60000 / 128) = 469 batches (completed on p.79).
concepts.significance: Implements the batching that fit did automatically on p.76.
concepts.example: Batch 0 = images[0:128], batch 1 = images[128:256], ... batch 468 = images[59904:60000] (96 samples).
concepts.misconception: The default batch_size of the generator (128) matches the fit call on p.76; it is a choice, not a requirement.

code.title: Building the mock Keras model

model = NaiveSequential(
    [
        NaiveDense(input_size=28 * 28, output_size=512, activation=ops.relu),
        NaiveDense(input_size=512, output_size=10, activation=ops.softmax),
    ]
)
assert len(model.weights) == 4

deeper.title: NaiveSequential vs keras.Sequential
deeper.body:
| | NaiveSequential (p.78) | keras.Sequential (p.76) |
|---|---|---|
| Layer list | stored in `self.layers` | stored internally |
| Forward pass | explicit loop in `__call__` | same idea, plus shape checks |
| Weights | `weights` property concatenating lists | `model.weights` / `trainable_weights` tracked automatically |
| Input size | must be passed to each NaiveDense | inferred on first call (`build()`, p.119) |
| Training | hand-written step (p.79) | `compile` + `fit` |

(Comparison compiled for these notes from p.76-p.78 and the chapter 3 passage on p.119.)

deeper.title: Tracing a batch through model(x)
deeper.body:
Let `x` have shape (128, 784).

1. `x = inputs` -> (128, 784)
2. First NaiveDense: `matmul(x, W1)` -> (128, 512); `+ b1` -> (128, 512); `relu` -> (128, 512)
3. Second NaiveDense: `matmul(x, W2)` -> (128, 10); `+ b2` -> (128, 10); `softmax` -> (128, 10), each row summing to 1
4. Return the (128, 10) probabilities.

misconceptions.claim: len(model.weights) == 4 means the model has 4 parameters.
misconceptions.correction: It has 4 weight tensors; together they contain 407,050 scalar parameters.

misconceptions.claim: NaiveSequential needs to know how each layer works internally.
misconceptions.correction: It only calls each layer on the previous output and reads its weights property; any callable with weights would work.

misconceptions.claim: The model's weights property copies the variables.
misconceptions.correction: It returns a list of the same variable objects, so updating these entries updates the layers themselves.

takeaways: NaiveDense exposes [W, b] through a weights property.
NaiveSequential applies its layers in order and concatenates their weights into one list.
The mock model 784 -> 512 (relu) -> 10 (softmax) reproduces the first example and has exactly 4 weight tensors.
A batch generator is needed to feed the model mini-batches of 128 samples; it is completed on p.79.

questions.question: Why does the assert check that len(model.weights) == 4?
options: Because each layer has two weight tensors (W and b) and there are two layers
Because the model has 4 output classes
Because relu and softmax each add two parameters
questions.answer: Because each layer has two weight tensors (W and b) and there are two layers
questions.explanation: model.weights concatenates [W1, b1] and [W2, b2]. The model has 10 output classes, trains for 5 epochs in the book, and activations have no parameters.

questions.question: List the shapes of the four tensors in model.weights, in order.
questions.explanation: W has shape (input_size, output_size) and b (output_size,); input_size=28*28=784 for the first layer and 512 for the second.

questions.question: How many scalar trainable parameters does the mock model contain?
questions.explanation: 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 for the first layer; 512*10 + 10 = 5,130 for the second; total 407,050.

questions.question: Why is it useful for the model to expose all its weights as a single flat list?
questions.answer: So the training step can compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight and apply an update to each, without knowing the model's structure.
questions.explanation: The page motivates the property as a way to keep track of the layers' parameters; p.79 then passes model.weights to the gradient and update functions.

questions.question: What does NaiveSequential.__call__ return for an input batch of shape (128, 784)?
options: A list of the outputs of each layer
questions.explanation: It feeds x through each layer and returns only the last output, which has 10 units. (128, 512) is the intermediate output of the first layer; it does not return a list.

questions.question: Why must NaiveDense be given input_size=28 * 28 explicitly, whereas layers.Dense(512) on p.76 needs no input size?
questions.answer: NaiveDense creates W in its constructor, before seeing any data, so it must know the input dimension; real Keras layers defer weight creation until they are first called and can read the input shape.
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 (p.119) explains this deferred build() mechanism for Keras layers.

questions.question: Could you add a third NaiveDense layer (e.g. 512 -> 256 -> 10) to the mock model? Which arguments must change and what would len(model.weights) be?
questions.answer: The second layer becomes NaiveDense(512, 256, relu) and a third NaiveDense(256, 10, softmax) is added; len(model.weights) == 6.
questions.explanation: Consecutive sizes must match, and each layer adds two weight tensors.
